questions.prompt: Share A trades 3 million shares a day; Share B trades 15,000. Which statement fits?

options.text: A 10,000-share order is harder to fill in B
options.explanation: Right: it is two thirds of B's daily volume but a tiny part of A's.

options.text: B has more liquidity, because fewer people own it
options.explanation: No: less trading usually means less liquidity.

options.text: Volume makes no difference to filling orders
options.explanation: No: thin volume can mean wider spreads and worse fills.

questions.prompt: Dividend 0.60 USD per share, EPS 0.80 USD, price 12.00 USD. What are the yield and the payout ratio?

options.explanation: No: that uses EPS instead of the dividend for the yield (0.80 ÷ 12.00), and turns the payout ratio upside down (0.80 ÷ 0.60).
No: these mix up the two formulas.

questions.prompt: A company reports profit up 8%. Buyers expected up 15%. Which is true?

options.text: The price must rise because profit grew
options.explanation: No: the price reacts to results compared with expectations.

options.text: The report has no effect on the price
options.explanation: No: prices often move sharply around reports.

options.text: The price may fall on the miss
options.explanation: Right: a miss against expectations can push the price down.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of style and main risk is right?

options.text: Value: the firm may be cheap for a reason
options.explanation: Right: a low price can reflect a shrinking business.

options.text: Growth: the dividend may turn out too high
options.explanation: No: the main growth risk is that growth slows while the price assumes it will not.

options.text: Long-term: no exit plan is needed at all
options.explanation: No: long-term investors still need to know what would make them sell.
